# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–14 (Complete – Updated 114)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Summer of fourth year in Mirecombe hill farms (earlier episodes); now **Brussels, Belgium, dawn of battle day—Regiment receives marching orders in early morning hours (French crossed Sambre, left already engaged, march in three hours). Waterloo campaign commencing.**
- **Earlier Timeline**: Spring of fourth year with Seena Orlwood drowned in flood; Winter of third year with frost on hedges; Evening at Brighton; Fine brilliant moonlight night of May; Army ordered to Belgium; Transports proceeded to Ostend; Amelia and Jos to Ramsgate; Now in Belgium in happy season transitioning to war; Famous Brussels ball evening of 15 June 1815 (historical); All Brussels in state of excitement.
- **Primary Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street counting-house, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers on Lombard Street, Long Acre), Brighton, Mirecombe, Wilhaven, Chatham (150th regiment mess, Mrs. O'Dowd's apartments, embarkation point), Harwich, Fulham (Mrs. Sedley's house, Mr. and Mrs. Clapp, Miss Flannigan), Ramsgate, Ostend, Brussels (Hotel de Ville, Park, Hotel du Parc—Rawdon and Rebecca's residence, opera-house, restaurateur's, Marshy aux Flures flower market, famous ball venue, Place of Arms with bugle signal), Belgium (flat flourishing country with green fields, quiet cities, chaussees, canal-boats, rich pastures, pleasant villages, old chateaux; Queen's Crawley riding-instruction location).

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Critical Action - Battle Announcement**: At play-table during ball aftermath, whispered to George: "The enemy has passed the Sambre, and our left is already engaged. Come away. We are to march in three hours." George responded with wild hurray, tossed off glass, walked away speedily on Dobbin's arm.
- **Earlier Actions**: Arrived Brighton via Slaughters' hotel; witnessed Stubble's tears; dined with officers. At Ship Inn: assumed jovial manner hiding feelings upon seeing Amelia; made clumsy compliments. In George's room: delivered disinheritance letter; George erupted; Dobbin offered financial support. At Chatham: wore shells on frockcoat, crimson sash and sabre; recognized Amelia; never spoke during Mrs. O'Dowd's party; took Jos home (maudlin); handed Amelia into carriage; she rebuked him smilingly; loitered smoking cigar watching George's windows; bought piano for Amelia's father's house at Fulham.
- **In Belgium**: "In a rage" at treatment of Amelia by Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Countess of Bareacres. Accompanied Jos and Amelia on carriage drives in Brussels Park. At opera: shrieked with laughter when Rebecca kissed fingers toward carriage, ran from box; shrieked out again when Mrs. O'Dowd mistakenly took compliment to herself and returned salute. Rebecca leaned on his arm when returning to her box (choosing him over George to "stay and talk to his dearest, best, little Amelia"). Expressed disapproval of Rebecca to George, calling her "a humbug" who "writhes and twists about like a snake." Few days after opera: remonstrated with George about giving up play. **Obtained invitation to famous Brussels ball through friendship with General commanding division. At ball: only person who came to disturb Amelia's unhappy thoughts; brought her refreshments and sat beside her. When Amelia clinging to him (called him by Christian name as George did), told him she was unwell and begged him to take her home; he went away with her quickly through crowds; her lodgings were hard by.**
- **Internal Conflict**: Deeply troubled by guilt over hastening marriage. Secret adoration of Amelia is his "greatest privilege and hope of life"; privately resolved he would not have let her go to Belgium if married to her. Knows Amelia considers him plain, awkward, ungainly. Now avoided by George in public and regiment.
- **Reputation**: "Greatly respected in the regiment, as the best officer and the cleverest man in it"

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Critical Actions - Battle Dawn**: At play-table: won repeatedly; said "Everything succeeds with me to-night"; restlessness persisted; pocketed winnings; went to buffet drinking many bumpers of wine. Upon Dobbin's news (enemy crossed Sambre, left engaged, march in three hours), gave wild hurray, tossed off glass, clapped it on table, walked away speedily. **Nerves quivering with excitement at news so long looked for; thought about thousand things—past life, future chances, fate before him, wife, child perhaps from whom unseen he might part. Wished night's work undone and could say farewell to tender and guileless being by whose love he had set such little store.** Thought over brief married life; in few weeks had frightfully dissipated little capital; had been wild and reckless. If mischance befall him, what left for her? How unworthy he was. Remembered father's generosity. Sat down and wrote farewell letter to father (remembering duel engagement letter reference). Dawn streaked sky as he closed letter; sealed it and kissed superscription; thought how he deserted generous father and thousand kindnesses stern old man had done him. **Had looked into Amelia's bedroom when entered; she lay quiet with eyes seemed closed; he was glad she was asleep. Upon arriving at quarters from ball, found regimental servant already making departure preparations (man understood signal to be still; arrangements made quickly and silently). Debated whether to wake Amelia or leave note for Jos to break news of departure. Went in to look at her once again. She had been awake when he first entered but kept eyes closed so wakefulness should not seem to reproach him. When he returned after herself, her timid heart felt more at ease; turning towards him as he stepped softly out, fell into light sleep. George came in and looked again, entering more softly. By pale night-lamp could see her sweet pale face—purple eyelids fringed and closed; one round arm smooth and white lay outside coverlet. He saw how pure, gentle, tender, friendless she was; how selfish, brutal, black with crime he was. Heart-stained and shame-stricken, stood at bed's foot looking at sleeping girl. Came to bedside, looked at little soft hand lying asleep; bent over pillow noiselessly toward gentle pale face.**
- **Earlier Status**: Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited (determination "final and irrevocable"). Receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Lost £140 to Rawdon at cards; obtained £2,000 cheque from Hulker and Bullock bankers; paid hotel bills with cheques. At Chatham: sent Amelia to mother with carte blanche; paid for everything requisite. At Brussels: ashamed of regiment, resolved to exchange to better regiment soon; takes wife to nightly jaunts; quite pleased with himself. Danced with Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Rebecca at ball. Called upon ladies; rode in Park; asked their party to dinner at restaurateur's. Purchased horse for private riding. Told Amelia Rebecca is comfort to "get rid of this damn'd Irishwoman" (Mrs. O'Dowd). **Carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; rides with her whenever free; pretends regimental business to Amelia (by which falsehood she not deceived); consigns wife to solitude or Jos's society; passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon; flatters himself wife "dying of love for him." At opera: claimed "We bear the same arms" to General Tufto (herald consultation fifteen years prior); Rebecca left his box giving "queerest, knowingest look" suggesting manipulation though George did not perceive it. After opera: Dobbin criticized Rebecca; George defended her as "nicest little woman in England," praised her shoulder and ability to "talk over Tufto in no time." Few days after opera: told Dobbin "we play low; I won last night" and suggested Crawley does not cheat; plays repeatedly with Crawley now. General Tufto dines abroad almost constantly; George always welcome in Crawley's apartments (very close to General's) in hotel.**
- **Relationship Status**: Nearly had first quarrel with Amelia over her unwillingness to visit Rebecca and high and mighty manner; George scolded Amelia violently; she did not reply but was bashful and awkward on second visit. Not quite six weeks married. Does not know Amelia is not suspicious (all his acquaintance perfectly aware).

**Amelia Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Critical Moment - Before Departure**: When George bent over her pillow at bedside in early morning, two fair arms closed tenderly round his neck as he stooped down. "I am awake, George," the poor child said, with a sob fit to break the little heart nestled so closely by his own. **At that moment bugle from Place of Arms began sounding clearly, taken up through town; amidst drums of infantry and shrill pipes of the Scotch, whole city awoke.**
- **Earlier Status**: Troubled by Rebecca's wit and misgivings about her. Rose early at Chatham; packed trunks with "greatest alacrity" while George lay in bed. Made "little disappointed curtsey" when George declined accompanying her to Fulham. Mother clasped her to heart with "all maternal eagerness and affection." Knelt seeking spiritual consolation; woke with smile in pavilion when George arrived. Bustling about completing outfit with great taste and elegant discernment. At Mrs. O'Dowd's party: quiet, good-natured, not too handsome; made agreeable impression; had "little triumph" which flushed spirits. Resolved to make all his friends welcome and make his home happy. Adopted by regiment with acclamation. **In Belgium: natural and unaffected; only amused by Mrs. O'Dowd's eccentricities. Letters home filled with delight and gratitude. Husband bade her buy laces, millinery, jewels; he kindest, best, most generous of men. At general's party: Countess of Bareacres would not answer when spoken to; Lady Blanche stared with eye-glass; Amelia wrote piteous accounts home. At opera: gentle eyes fixed anxiously on Rebecca and George; embraced Rebecca with affectionate rapture. Overpowered by flash, dazzle, fashionable talk of worldly rival. When visited Rawdon and Rebecca's quarters: displayed evident unwillingness and high and mighty manner; George scolded her violently; she silent but more bashful and awkward on second visit. Not quite six weeks married. Aware George carrying on flirtation with Rebecca; does not plague him with jealousy but becomes unhappy and pines miserably in secret. At Brussels ball: did not know soul; sat quite unnoticed in corner after George placed her on bench except when Rawdon came with clumsy conversation and Dobbin brought refreshments. Alarmed by Rebecca telling her George would go on playing. Witnessing Rebecca's request to George for scarf and flowers proved "quite too much for her"; suddenly clinging to Dobbin called him by Christian name, begging him to take her home; went away with him quickly through crowds; did not sleep although din, clatter, galloping of horsemen incessant; never heard noises having quite other disturbances.**

**Mrs. Major Peggy O'Dowd** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- One of five sisters and eleven children of Glenmalony; Mick O'Dowd married her after she tried nine seasons at Dublin and two at Bath and Cheltenham. Carried to West Indies; now in Belgium as entertaining companion. In Brussels: continually prattles about Ballinasloe, Dublin cattle, markets, Glenmalony. Cock's plume in hat and large repeater on stomach which she rings on all occasions (presented by fawther as she stepped into carriage after marriage). **Not invited to Brussels ball; panted to be asked; strove in vain to procure tickets; made Jos envious when Dobbin displayed invitation. At opera: wore splendid Irish diamonds and Cairngorms; tossed about fan with splendid complacency; when Rebecca performed hand-kissing, Mrs. O'Dowd mistakenly took compliment to herself and returned gracious smile, sending Dobbin shrieking from box. Rebecca admired her brooch and diamonds, wouldn't believe they were not from Golconda direct. Made timely observation when neither lady rallied ("Why didn't you BOY one?" regarding bouquets); became silent and subdued afterward, silenced by Rebecca's flash and dazzle.** **Upon hearing Major's information that regiment will march next morning (implied by his words), became very grave. Major told her to wake him half an hour before assembly beats, call him at half-past one, prepare his things; may be he'll not come back to breakfast (signifying regiment will march next morning). After regiment's departure, betook herself to large volume of uncle the Dean's sermons for meditation; perhaps did not understand much; thoughts were elsewhere; sleep project with poor Mick's nightcap on pillow was quite vain one. She who remains and suffers—has leisure to think, brood, remember.**

**Major Mick O'Dowd** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Served sovereign in every quarter of world; paid for every step by acts of daring and gallantry. Most modest, silent, sheep-faced, meek of little men; obedient to wife. **Upon understanding regiment will march next morning, placidly pulled nightcap over his ears, told Peggy: "that there will be such a ball danced in a day or two as some of 'em has never heard the chune of"; much more happy to retire to rest after quiet tumbler than figure at other sort of amusement. Asked to be woken half an hour before assembly beats, called at half-past one, things ready; may be he'll not come back to breakfast; words signified opinion that regiment would march next morning; ceased talking and fell asleep.**

**Jos Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Earlier Status**: Arrived Chatham in fine carriage with Amelia; recognized Dobbin; attended Mrs. O'Dowd's party in maudlin state; told tiger-hunt story. Agreed to escort Amelia and Mrs. O'Dowd abroad; ceased shaving upper lip; followed parades and drills with great assiduity; received excellent assistance from Mrs. O'Dowd in military studies. Made appearance in braided frock-coat and duck trousers, foraging cap with smart gold band. **In Belgium**: Interposed about curry and rice; owned with sigh that England had no equal for good streaky beef despite Mrs. O'Dowd's assertions. Hired pair of horses for open carriage in Brussels; made tolerable figure in drives about Park. Accompanied Amelia on carriage drives; more at ease when great man (General Tufto with Rebecca) departed. Referenced Battle of Salamanca. At opera: eating ice; Rebecca admired Jos with "kindliest greeting." **At Brussels ball: panting to be asked with Mrs. O'Dowd; strove in vain to procure tickets; made Jos envious when Dobbin displayed invitation obtained through General commanding division.**

**John Osborne (Old Mr. Osborne)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Wealthy merchant; George's father; savage, determined man. Upon learning George married Amelia, erupted in fury. Locked himself in study; retrieved mahogany escritoire; examined George's documents with "curses quivering on livid lips" and "horrid hatred and disappointment"; marked, docketed, catalogued with dates. Commissioned lawyer to draft letter stating determination "final and irrevocable." George ceases to be family member. In London, news how son is entertaining peers and peeresses came to Osborne's ears in the City. **George now wrote farewell letter to him, remembering his past generosity and thousand kindnesses, with dawn streaking sky; sealed and kissed superscription.**

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Secretly married to Rawdon; heavily indebted. All reconciliation attempts with Miss Crawley permanently rebuffed; successfully reconciled with Miss Briggs on beach. Sent crumpled note to Rawdon requesting money from "Cupid" (George); Rawdon extracted considerable payment; remarked "comfortable inn in Brighton is better than spunging-house in Chancery Lane." Packed chief valuables sent to London under care of George's servant. **In Belgium**: Now in Brussels with Rawdon and General Tufto at Hotel du Parc. Encountered Osborne party in Park riding on beautiful little Arab in prettiest tightest riding-habit (acquired art at Queen's Crawley); accompanied by General Tufto amid greatest persons in Brussels. Acknowledged Amelia graciously with nod, smile, playful finger-kissing. At opera: performed hand-kissing toward Amelia's box; clapped hands together when George entered her box; General Tufto's presence noted—he stared at George with sulky scowl. Rebecca left box leaning on Dobbin's arm (choosing him over George). During her time in Amelia's box, bustled, chattered, turned and twisted, smiled upon one, smirked on another; admired Mrs. O'Dowd's Cairngorm brooch and Irish diamonds. After opera, General Tufto cursed "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; curses came from heart; was jealous and angry about Rebecca and George together. Osborne and Crawley repeatedly together now; George always welcome in their apartments. When Amelia and George visited, Amelia displayed evident unwillingness and high and mighty manner toward Rebecca; nearly caused first quarrel; George scolded Amelia violently; Amelia bashful and awkward on second visit. Rebecca remarked to George: thought Amelia jealous at Brighton; now supposes scandalised because Rawdon, Rebecca, and General live together; questioned how they could live without friend to share expenses; claimed she was "very much obliged to Emmy, very"; revealed General ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours"; pert toss of head; invited George to dinner; General dines with Commander-in-Chief. **At Brussels ball: invited; danced with George twice or thrice; made request to George for scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in last few days). Later at hotel after ball: Rebecca and Rawdon discussed financial schemes—Rebecca saying "we have not done with your aunt yet; if she fails us, isn't there what you call the Gazette? or when your uncle Bute's life drops, I have another scheme. Living has always belonged to younger brother, why shouldn't you sell out and go into the Church?" Idea of conversion set Rawdon into roars of laughter (explosion heard through hotel at midnight); General Tufto heard haw-haws of great dragoon's voice from quarters on first floor above them; Rebecca acted scene with great spirit and preached Rawdon's first sermon to immense delight of General at breakfast.**

**Rawdon Crawley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Secretly married to Rebecca; heavily indebted. Extracted considerable payment from George in bank-notes and bill on agents; lost £140 to George at cards. Met Miss Crawley when she took air in chair; she held out couple of fingers; Rawdon turned red as scarlet. Miss Crawley subsequently disparaged his appearance. **In Belgium**: Now in Brussels lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rebecca and General Tufto. Encountered Osborne party in park; shook hands heartily with Amelia and spoke warmly to Jos; stared at Mrs. O'Dowd's face and black cock's feathers until she thought she made conquest. Sent message to George at opera inviting him to dinner Tuesday when General dines out; asked George to "make Sedley cut off his moustache." Said "Hm, as you please" when George expressed intention to pay respects to Rebecca alone, looking very glum; two young officers exchanged knowing glances. Repeatedly together with George now; George always welcome in quarters. **Lets Osborne come and go with entire good humour; understood perfectly well with Rebecca (though never absolutely conspired in so many words) that one cajoled young gentleman whilst other won his money at cards; understood winning money from Osborne while flattering himself wife dying of love for him. After ball: roared with laughter at Rebecca's Church conversion idea, explosion heard through hotel at midnight, haw-haws of great dragoon's voice audible, General Tufto heard from quarters above.**

**General Tufto** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Military officer in Brussels with considerable status. Lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rawdon and Rebecca. Dines out almost constantly; Tuesday mentioned as occasion dining with Commander-in-Chief. **At opera: stared at George with sulky scowl when George entered Rebecca's box; disengaged eye working round in Rebecca's direction, shooting out bloodshot glances at her and George; when Rebecca left box with George, gave low utterance to curses "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; curses came from heart; was jealous and angry; ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours" (Amelia). Capable of generating such lust and fury, rage and hatred. Heard roars of laughter from Rawdon and Rawdon's haw-haws through hotel at midnight (Rebecca's Church conversion scene preached to him at breakfast, to immense delight).**

## Critical Facts and Status

**WATERLOO CAMPAIGN - BATTLE COMMENCES AT DAWN**: French have crossed Sambre; British left already engaged. **Regiment receives marching orders in early morning hours—to march in three hours.** Dobbin brings news to George at play-table during ball aftermath. Bugle from Place of Arms signals at dawn as George stands at Amelia's bedside; taken up through town; drums of infantry and shrill pipes of Scotch awaken whole Brussels. **Major O'Dowd indicates regiment will march next morning; asks to be woken at half-past one; may not return to breakfast. After regiment's departure, Mrs. O'Dowd betakes herself to Dean's sermon volume for meditation and sorrow, leisure to think and brood and remember.**

**GEORGE-AMELIA MARRIAGE - FRACTURED AT CRITICAL MOMENT**: Married late April; disinherited "final and irrevocable"; obtained £2,000 cheque; receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Not quite six weeks married. **George carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; rides with her whenever free; pretends regimental business to Amelia (by which falsehood she not deceived); consigns wife to solitude or Jos's society; passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon; flatters himself wife "dying of love for him." Amelia aware but does not plague him with jealousy; becomes unhappy and pines miserably in secret. Does not know Amelia is not suspicious (all acquaintance perfectly aware). At Brussels ball: George left Amelia unnoticed on bench; danced with Rebecca twice or thrice; came at Rebecca's request for scarf and flowers twenty times in last few days. Amelia found this "quite too much"; clung to Dobbin, called him by Christian name, begged him to take her home; did not sleep that night. Nearly had first quarrel over Amelia's unwillingness to visit Rebecca; George scolded her violently; she silent but bashful and awkward on second visit.**

**GEORGE'S REMORSE AND FAREWELL**: At play-table after news of battle, thought "Everything succeeds with me to-night"; won repeatedly; restlessness persisted; drank many bumpers of wine. Upon Dobbin's announcement, nerves quivered with excitement at long-looked-for news. **Thought about thousand things—past life, future chances, fate before him, wife, child perhaps from whom unseen he might part. Wished night's work undone and could say farewell to tender and guileless being by whose love he had set such little store. Thought over brief married life; in few weeks had frightfully dissipated little capital; had been wild and reckless. If mischance befall him, what left for her? How unworthy he was. Remembered father's generosity and thousand kindnesses. Sat down and wrote farewell letter to father (remembering duel engagement letter reference). Dawn streaked sky as he closed letter; sealed and kissed superscription. Regimental servant already making departure preparations (arrangements made quickly and silently). Debated whether to wake Amelia or leave note for Jos. Went in to look at her once again. She had been awake when he first entered but kept eyes closed so wakefulness should not seem to reproach him. When he returned after herself, her timid heart felt more at ease; she turned towards him, fell into light sleep. George came in and looked again, entering more softly. By pale night-lamp could see her sweet pale face, purple eyelids fringed and closed, one round arm smooth and white lay outside coverlet. He saw how pure, gentle, tender, friendless she was; how selfish, brutal, black with crime he was. Heart-stained and shame-stricken, stood at bed's foot. Came to bedside, looked at little soft hand; bent over pillow noiselessly toward gentle pale face. Two fair arms closed tenderly round his neck as he stooped down. "I am awake, George," the poor child said, with a sob fit to break the little heart nestled so closely by his own. At that moment bugle from Place of Arms began sounding clearly, taken up through town; amidst drums and pipes, whole city awoke.**

**REBECCA-RAWDON-GENERAL TUFTO TRIANGLE - VOLATILE, MANIPULATIVE**: Both Rawdon and Rebecca in Brussels at Hotel du Parc with General Tufto; precarious finances ongoing. **General deeply jealous of George and Rebecca; at opera cursed with intense rage and fury after Rebecca left box with George. Rawdon and Rebecca understand each other perfectly: one cajoled young gentleman while other won money at cards; George not perceiving manipulation. After ball: Rebecca and Rawdon discussed financial schemes (Gazette, Church conversion idea); Rawdon roared with laughter, explosion heard through hotel at midnight, haw-haws audible to General Tufto on first floor above, who heard them at breakfast with immense delight (Rebecca preached Rawdon's first sermon for his entertainment). General dines abroad almost constantly (away from Hotel du Parc). George always welcome in their apartments.**
